raw_response: {"sentences":[{"text":"From Square du Vert-Galant, carry on toward the Conciergerie, about a nine-minute walk.","source_id":"GLUE_NAV","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Just back there, on that green tip of the island, the last Grand Master of the Templars, Jacques de Molay, was burnt at the stake — and as the flames took him, he cursed the kings of France.","source_id":"GLUE_REFLECTION","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":2},{"text":"As you cross to the island, look across from the Henri IV statue — those red-brick seventeenth-century houses frame the entrance to place Dauphine, one of the city's most secluded and lovely squares.","source_id":"f9dc74d3-019a-436f-9669-fb84e647755c","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Outside the Conciergerie, look up at the Tour de l'Horloge, built around 1350 to carry Paris's first public clock.","source_id":"afb6be5c-8ac7-4312-97ad-68bdf9b532ba","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Now the dark part.","source_id":"b2316d07-e65e-418b-98d2-a4252e3171b4","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"In the fifteenth century, passers-by could still hear the screams of tortured prisoners coming from the Tour Bonbec, the westernmost tower, and its name comes from bon-bec — old French for prate, for chatter — a grim nod to the interrogations on the ground floor, where every kind of torture was devised to wring out confessions and denunciations.","source_id":"b2316d07-e65e-418b-98d2-a4252e3171b4","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"When the tower was restored in 1828, workers found two oubliettes in the basement: hidden dungeons spiked with iron points and opening straight onto the river.","source_id":"b2316d07-e65e-418b-98d2-a4252e3171b4","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"You can guess what became of the prisoners dropped into them.","source_id":"b2316d07-e65e-418b-98d2-a4252e3171b4","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"This is Paris's oldest prison, one of the few surviving pieces of the medieval Palais de Justice.","source_id":"e31a54a4-1e8b-4193-b2aa-5fdc8fab4966","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Inside are vaulted Gothic halls, the grandest being the Salle des Gens d'Armes, which went up between 1301 and 1315.","source_id":"e31a54a4-1e8b-4193-b2aa-5fdc8fab4966","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"At the far end, an iron grille once penned off the pailleux — prisoners too poor to bribe a guard for a cell of their own, left to sleep on straw, on paille.","source_id":"e31a54a4-1e8b-4193-b2aa-5fdc8fab4966","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Beyond it runs a corridor where prisoners were let to wander freely, and among the rebuilt rooms is the salle de toilette, where the condemned had their hair cropped and their shirt collars torn off, ready for the guillotine.","source_id":"f3817861-6520-4bbe-8263-790afa3b11dd","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"During the Revolution the cells here held an extraordinary roll of the doomed.","source_id":"575ca557-acb3-419b-ba84-2917fcf07805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"There was Madame Roland, who'd backed the Revolution but sided with the Girondins at exactly the wrong moment.","source_id":"575ca557-acb3-419b-ba84-2917fcf07805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"And there was Marie-Antoinette, who sat in a dreary cell from the 2nd of August to the 16th of October 1793, before they took her to the guillotine on the Place de la Révolution — the Place de la Concorde today.","source_id":"575ca557-acb3-419b-ba84-2917fcf07805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2,"also_cites":["e31a54a4-1e8b-4193-b2aa-5fdc8fab4966"]},{"text":"Then, one after another, came Danton, Robespierre, and Saint-Just, with Danton and Robespierre in the cells right next to the Queen's.","source_id":"575ca557-acb3-419b-ba84-2917fcf07805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"People come now for the history, but the Gothic halls and the great kitchen fireplaces are worth it for the stonework alone.","source_id":"575ca557-acb3-419b-ba84-2917fcf07805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Up on the top floor there's a mock-up of Marie-Antoinette's cell, her crucifix hanging forlorn against peeling fleur-de-lys wallpaper.","source_id":"2560212a-79e9-487c-8b0f-300b7465b06c","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"North of the halls ran the stretch leading to the dark cells, called the rue de Paris, after the Great Executioner himself, Monsieur de Paris.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"That title stayed in one family, the Sansons, for seven generations, passed father to son from 1688 to 1847.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Just before the Revolution, Louis XVI had set out to better the executioners' lot, granting Charles-Henri Sanson a yearly fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns to keep up the scaffold and pillory — never dreaming the same man would one day be his own executioner.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Charles-Henri was a royalist and had no stomach for the deed.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"On the 15th of August 1792 he was arrested as \"the despot's employee,\" and for each execution he was marched from his cell to the Place du Carrousel, where the guillotine then stood, then marched back.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"At first the killings were few, but once the blade was working at full swing and his expert hand couldn't be spared, they let him go.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"He retired soon after he'd executed his own sovereign.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"His son Henri carried the post through the Terror and every shaky regime that followed, right up to 1840, deep into the reign of Louis-Philippe.","source_id":"63007efd-b494-424c-861d-4b1671139ec9","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"And here's the strange thread that ties all of this to living memory: the film-maker Jean Renoir marvelled that his own grandfather, the painter Renoir's father, a tailor from Limoges, had known Henri Sanson's chief assistant during the Terror.","source_id":"87368cec-a35c-49ad-81f4-920fd0add7a8","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"That old assistant, Renoir wrote, \"may have passed Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin in the street, heard Mozart play the harpsichord, and attended performances of Monsieur Beaumarchais.\"","source_id":"87368cec-a35c-49ad-81f4-920fd0add7a8","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"Old Renoir met him in 1845 — the year the family moved up to Paris from Limoges, and the last Sanson still held the post.","source_id":"87368cec-a35c-49ad-81f4-920fd0add7a8","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"The two became friends, the tailor and the executioner's assistant, united by the plain pleasure of doing a good job.","source_id":"87368cec-a35c-49ad-81f4-920fd0add7a8","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2},{"text":"\"After all,\" Jean Renoir observed, \"they were two good workmen: one cut out cloth, the other cut off heads just as conscientiously.\"","source_id":"87368cec-a35c-49ad-81f4-920fd0add7a8","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":2}]}
